title: Ring objects of abelian sheaves
statement:
A *ring object* of a monoidal category $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1)$ is a monoid
object. It consists of an object $R$, a *multiplication* $\mu\colon R\otimes R\to R$ and
a *unit* $\eta\colon\mathbf 1\to R$, such that $\mu$ is associative,
$\mu\circ(\mu\otimes\mathrm{id})=\mu\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{R,R,R}$, and
$\eta$ is a two-sided unit, $\mu\circ(\eta\otimes\mathrm{id})=\lambda_R$ and
$\mu\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes\eta)=\rho_R$. A *morphism of ring objects* is a morphism
compatible with the multiplications and the units. If $\mathcal C$ is braided, the ring
object $R$ is *commutative* when $\mu\circ\beta_{R,R}=\mu$.

Throughout, $\Ab$ carries the tensor product $\otimes_{\mathbf Z}$ with unit $\mathbf Z$.
For a site $C$ whose underlying category is essentially small, abelian presheaves carry
the objectwise tensor product, and abelian sheaves carry the sheafified objectwise tensor
product: for abelian sheaves $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$,

$$
\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal G:=a\bigl(U\longmapsto\mathcal F(U)\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathcal G(U)\bigr),
$$

with unit $a(\underline{\mathbf Z})$, where $a$ denotes sheafification. This applies,
for example, to $X_{\mathrm{proét}}$ and to the site of profinite sets with the coherent
topology.

1. Every ring $R$ is a ring object of $\Ab$, with unit $\mathbf Z\to R$, $n\mapsto n\cdot1$,
   and multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbf Z}R\to R$, $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. A ring
   homomorphism is a morphism of ring objects. If $R$ is commutative, so is the ring
   object $R$.
2. A presheaf of rings $P$ on $C$ is, objectwise as in 1, a ring object of abelian
   presheaves, and a morphism of presheaves of rings is a morphism of ring objects. The
   sheafification $aP$ of the underlying abelian presheaf is a ring object of
   $\Sh(C,\Ab)$, commutative when all the rings $P(U)$ are.
3. The abelian sheaf underlying a sheaf of rings $\mathcal R$ on $C$ is a ring object of
   $\Sh(C,\Ab)$, commutative when all the rings $\mathcal R(U)$ are. A morphism of sheaves
   of rings is a morphism of ring objects.

proof.text: Use the monoid-object definition of [det-def-sfb-ring-object-monoid] for the initial paragraph: its multiplication, unit, associativity and two unit equations are exactly the displayed equations here. Its morphisms preserve multiplication and unit, and its braided commutativity condition is exactly $\mu\circ\beta_{R,R}=\mu$. The tensor products and units in the second paragraph are those of [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor], specialized to $\mathcal A=\Ab$; all sites below have the size convention stipulated there.

source.place: Initial two paragraphs: monoid objects and the fixed tensor products

proof.text: For clause 1, [det-def-sfb-ring-object-rings] supplies the object $(R,\mu_R,\eta_R)$ with precisely $\mu_R(a\otimes b)=ab$ and $\eta_R(n)=n\cdot1$, including its ring-object laws. Its second clause supplies preservation of the two structure maps by every ring homomorphism, and its third supplies commutativity when $R$ is commutative. Thus this is the construction of clause 1 with all its stated functoriality, for arbitrary unital rings, including the zero ring.

For the presheaf part of clause 2, at $U$ take the maps of step 2 for $P(U)$. For a restriction $r:P(U)\to P(V)$, the identities $r(ab)=r(a)r(b)$ and $r(n\cdot1)=n\cdot1$ say exactly that these multiplication and unit maps are natural. The ring-object equations hold after evaluation at every $U$ by [det-def-sfb-ring-object-rings]. Since the presheaf tensor, associator, unitors and symmetry are objectwise, as stated in [det-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor-presheaf], these are the required equations of natural transformations. A presheaf ring map has components preserving multiplication and unit by step 2, hence does so as a natural transformation. If each $P(U)$ is commutative, the commutativity equation holds at every $U$ as well.

source.place: Clause 2, first sentence: objectwise ring-object structure

proof.text: For the sheafification part of clause 2, [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor] makes $a$ a strong symmetric monoidal functor. Apply [det-def-sfb-ring-object-transport] to the presheaf ring object just constructed. Its multiplication is $aP\otimes aP\xrightarrow{\sim}a(P\otimes_pP)\xrightarrow{a\mu_P}aP$, and its unit is $\underline{\mathbf Z}=a(\underline{\mathbf Z})\xrightarrow{a\eta_P}aP$, where the underlined integer object inside $a$ is the constant presheaf and the one outside is the constant sheaf. Clause 1 of the transport statement gives the ring-object laws and preservation of morphisms; clause 2 gives commutativity because a symmetric monoidal functor is braided. These are precisely the remaining assertions about $aP$.

source.place: Clause 2, second sentence: strong symmetric monoidal sheafification

proof.text: For clause 3 use [det-def-sfb-ring-object-sheaf], whose statement gives both that $S=\mathcal R_{\Ab}$ is a sheaf and that the counit $c:aS\xrightarrow{\sim}S$ identifies its ring structure with that on $aS$ constructed in step 4. Explicitly, if $(m,e)$ are the structure maps on $aS$, take $\mu_S=c\circ m\circ(c^{-1}\otimes c^{-1})$ and $\eta_S=c\circ e$. The cited statement identifies these maps with the unique extensions of the sectionwise product and of $n\mapsto n\cdot1$; thus the construction uses the actual underlying abelian sheaf. It also gives commutativity when the section rings are commutative. For completeness, preservation by a sheaf ring map $f:S\to T$ can be read directly from that extension characterization: both $f\mu_S$ and $\mu_T(f\otimes f)$ extend the presheaf map $(a,b)\mapsto f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$, so uniqueness of extension makes them equal; similarly $f\eta_S=\eta_T$ because $f(n\cdot1)=n\cdot1$. This proves the morphism assertion without assuming that the inclusion of abelian sheaves into presheaves is strong monoidal.

source.place: Clause 3: underlying abelian sheaf, counit transport and morphisms
